title: ARP & Address Resolution
summary: See how a host maps an IP address to a MAC address on its local network, and why ARP's trust-by-default design creates a real, exploitable weakness.

slides.markdown: Your OS knows a destination's IP address; the network interface can only send to a MAC address. **ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)** is the glue that maps one to the other on a local network — and because it trusts any reply by default, it's also one of the oldest exploitable weaknesses in networking.

An application only ever deals in IP addresses — it asks the OS to send data to `192.168.1.20`. But an Ethernet frame can only be addressed by MAC, so before the frame can be built, the sending host needs to know: **what MAC address is behind this IP, on my local segment?**

This is purely a local-network problem — once a packet leaves the LAN via a router, the next hop repeats the same resolution for its own segment, using its own ARP.

The resolution itself is a simple broadcast-then-unicast exchange:

![ARP request broadcast to the whole LAN, answered by a unicast reply only from the matching host](assets/arp-request-reply.svg)

Host A broadcasts "who has this IP?" to everyone; only the host that owns it replies directly, and A caches the answer for future frames.

assets.alt: ARP request broadcast to the whole LAN, answered by a unicast reply only from the matching host

slides.markdown:
Each host keeps an **ARP cache** — a table of recently resolved IP-to-MAC mappings — so it doesn't have to broadcast a request for every single packet. Entries carry a short **TTL** (commonly tens of seconds to a few minutes, OS-dependent) and expire automatically, since a device's MAC-to-IP binding can change (new NIC, DHCP reassignment).

You can inspect this cache directly (`arp -a` on most OSes) — it's often the first thing to check when diagnosing "why can't I reach this device on my LAN," alongside `ping`/`traceroute`.

A **gratuitous ARP** is a host announcing its own IP-to-MAC mapping *unprompted* — no one asked. Legitimate uses:

- **Failover** — a backup server taking over a virtual IP announces "this IP is now at my MAC" so every host updates its cache immediately, without waiting for individual requests.
- **Conflict detection** — a device booting up announces its own IP; if another device replies claiming the same IP, that's a duplicate-address conflict, caught early.

The same unsolicited-announcement mechanism that makes failover fast is exactly what an attacker abuses in ARP spoofing (next).

ARP has **no authentication** — any device can send an ARP reply (or gratuitous ARP) claiming to own any IP address, and hosts trust it by default. **ARP spoofing** exploits exactly this: an attacker sends forged replies telling Host A "the gateway's MAC is mine" and telling the gateway "Host A's MAC is mine."

Both sides update their caches, and traffic that should flow directly between A and the gateway now silently routes through the attacker first — the foundation of a classic on-LAN man-in-the-middle attack.

Poisoning both directions turns a passive listener into an active man-in-the-middle:

![An attacker sending forged ARP replies to both a victim and the gateway, inserting itself into all their traffic](assets/arp-spoofing-mitm.svg)

The attacker forwards traffic on (nothing looks broken) while quietly reading or modifying it — why this is dangerous on shared, untrusted LANs like public Wi-Fi.

assets.alt: An attacker sending forged ARP replies to both a victim and the gateway, inserting itself into all their traffic

slides.markdown:
Two practical defenses:

- **Static ARP entries** — manually fix critical IP-to-MAC mappings (e.g. the default gateway) so a spoofed reply can't overwrite them. Doesn't scale to large networks, but effective for a handful of critical hosts.
- **Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)** — a switch feature that validates ARP replies against a trusted binding table (often built from DHCP snooping), dropping forged ones before they ever reach a host.

Encryption (HTTPS, VPNs) doesn't prevent the spoofing itself, but it does limit what an attacker sitting in the middle can actually read or tamper with.

slides.subTitle: Both "resolve names," but nothing else is alike
slides.markdown:
A common mistake is lumping ARP and DNS together because both "resolve an address." They operate at very different scopes: ARP resolves IP → MAC, purely **local** to one LAN segment, with no hierarchy. DNS resolves hostname → IP, **globally**, hierarchically (root → TLD → authoritative), with caching across the whole internet.

An ARP cache entry is meaningless outside your local segment; a DNS record is meaningless without the query hierarchy behind it. Don't reach for DNS concepts when reasoning about ARP — it's a much simpler, purely-local protocol.
